catalog_quote: However, such a restriction might be a consequence of a more general constraint stipulating that no content word has an stressed open syllable with a short vowel. Thus, it seems that the occurrence of Falling tone depends, at least partially, on prosodic conditions, such that only the syllable of a word with primary stress is able to bear the contour. The YZ tone pattern is unconstrained regarding the ability of realizing Falling tones in every syllable that is licensed to contrast tone. [p. 166] ... Some data suggest that the the permissible weight of the nucleus in the stressed syllable of content words (particularly, those in root and stems) is two moras. [p. 132] ... Figure 25. Bimoraic syllable structure of stressed syllables in content words. [p. 133] ... The major generalization is that a borrowed word in YZ will take the stressed syllable of the Spanish word as the locus of the borrowing. Thus, regardless of the two possible stress patterns in bisyllabic Spanish words—with initial or final stress—without exception the stressed syllable corresponds to the YZ borrowed word. [p. 153]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Yalálag Zapotec is a tone language (High, Low, Falling). Avelino gives no explicit stress-placement rule; his statements presuppose one stressed (primary-stress) syllable per content word, which is the root/stem syllable: roots are typically monosyllabic, the stressed nucleus is bimoraic (long vowel, diphthong, or vowel plus coda), and only the primary-stressed syllable can carry Falling tone. Bisyllabic Spanish loans are transcribed with stress on the syllable that was stressed in Spanish (e.g. ka'ba3, ku'pad, pan'dank, sep'tjembr, p. 154), which ends up as the word-final/stem syllable. Provisionally: stress is morphologically fixed on the (usually monosyllabic) root/stem syllable, not on affixes or clitics; a positional label cannot be assigned from this source.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only one remark: the infinitive prefix w- before vowel-initial stems is 'a very short gesture, without independent (secondary) stress' and is not parsed as a separate syllable (p. 144).
new_statements.exceptions: Loan word par'jid < Spanish pálido is called 'still problematic' because Spanish stress is initial but the YZ form keeps the final syllable (p. 156). No native-word exceptions discussed.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern content words/roots and stems (lexical word level) and loanword adaptation; no discussion of phrase-level accent. Tone, not stress, is the contrastive prosody; stress is treated as a prosodic condition on tone-bearing and syllable weight.
new_statements.identity_note: Avelino 2004 describes the Zapotec of Villa Hidalgo Yalálag itself (speakers recorded in Yalálag and in the Los Angeles diaspora), i.e. yala1267/zpu proper. Hernández Andrade 2011 describes two varieties spoken in San Juan Jaltepec (Choapan district), one of Yalálag origin and one of Santa María Yahuivé/Choapan origin (zpc); it contains no stress statement.

tone_statements.quote: Yalálag Zapotec has three tones: high, low and falling. A number of factors indicate the phonemic status of the three tones, and especially that of the contour tone. First, they enter in contrastive relations, so that there are minimal pairs for tone. … the three tones are the maximum of tone contrasts found in the tone system. Additional contours –falling and rising– and tone adjustments, such as upstep and downstep, might arise as the result of morphological and intonational processes. High and low tones are essentially realized as level …
tone_statements.summary: Three phonemic tones with minimal pairs: high and low (both realized as level) and a falling contour; further contours and upstep/downstep may arise from morphological and intonational processes.
